facts.fact: Jacques Pellegrin described Tetraodon schoutedeni in 1926.
The original description appeared in Revue de Zoologie Africaine and was based on specimens Dr. Schouteden collected in the Belgian Congo.
The type locality is Kinshasa (Leopoldville), Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The species is named after Henri Schouteden, a Belgian zoologist.
It belongs to the genus Tetraodon in the pufferfish family Tetraodontidae.
The body is slightly rounded and globular and tapers toward the tail.
The body is light brownish-green with black spots.
The skin has no scales, and its colour can change with conditions and stress.
Its eyes move largely independently of each other.
It has a beak of fused teeth for cracking prey.
It can inflate its body as a defence.
It contains tetrodotoxin, though it is described as much less toxic than some relatives.
FishBase lists it as harmless to humans.
The IUCN lists it as Data Deficient (assessed 16 February 2009).
It lives only in fresh water, unlike most pufferfish.
It is a fully freshwater river species that never needs salt.
The keepers in the video say its teeth grow much more slowly than other puffers' teeth and need no trimming.
Wikipedia says its teeth grow continuously and must be worn down with hard foods such as snail shells.
It is native to the Congo River basin in Africa.
FishBase reports it from large rivers of the Congo basin, apparently only from Pool Malebo (Kinshasa).
Wikipedia gives its range mainly as the Ubangi River basin and the Lua River.
The video says it comes from the lower Congo River basin.
One hobbyist source places it in the lower–middle Congo Basin, centred on Pool Malebo between Kinshasa and Brazzaville.
It lives on the bottom of large rivers and is not a brackish-water species.
Pool Malebo is described as warm, soft water with a low mineral content.
It is said to use shallow shore zones with sandy or muddy bottoms, submerged plants, roots and woody debris.
Other freshwater puffer species live alongside it in the lower Congo basin.
It is traded commercially as an aquarium fish.
In the 1960s it was among the most commonly kept freshwater puffers and was often bred in captivity.
Wild exports fell during the Congo Crisis and later civil wars, and it almost disappeared from the hobby.
Wild-caught exports have resumed and captive breeding has grown, and its popularity has risen sharply since about 2018.
The video says it cost about $5 in the 1960s and 1970s, but unrest in its home region has since made it expensive and its supply patchy.
Captive breeding programmes are reported in America, Germany and Indonesia.
The keepers in the video say it can live its whole life in a 40-gallon breeder tank.
For one adult, the recommended minimum footprint is about 80 x 35 cm with a water depth of about 40 cm.
For a group of six, the recommended tank is at least 120 x 45 cm with a water depth of 50 cm.
FishBase gives 22–26 °C, pH 6.5–7.5 and dH 10–20.
The video recommends 75–82 °F and pH 6.5–8 in a mature, stable tank.
One hobbyist care sheet recommends 26–27.5 °C, pH 6.5–7.5 and 4–10 dGH.
In the wild it eats bottom-living animals such as snails and worms.
In the wild it also eats insect larvae.
In the aquarium, sources recommend snails, earthworms and insects; some keepers also succeed with bloodworms and prepared foods.
The keepers in the video say snails make up about 95% of the diet and that it always takes bloodworms.
One care sheet suggests a diet of about half snails, 15% earthworms and 10% insects and larvae.
FishBase describes it as solitary and aggressive toward its own kind.
Wikipedia calls its peaceful reputation a misconception and says it can attack without provocation.
Wikipedia recommends keeping it alone or in a group of at least six with about two females per male.
The keepers in the video found it community-safe and saw no aggression toward tankmates such as Congo tetras, barbs and small cichlids.
The video describes it as personable and intelligent, and says it follows its owner at feeding time.
One care sheet calls it inquisitive and fairly peaceful, but warns that it is unpredictable and not a safe community fish.
Females grow larger and rounder than males, which stay more streamlined.
Males reportedly have a shorter snout and darker spots along the cheek.
One care sheet gives females 9–10 cm and males 7–8 cm, and says colour is not a reliable way to sex them.
FishBase says eggs are laid on leaves and the male sometimes guards them.
Wikipedia says courtship starts with tandem swimming, and the male bites and clings to the female before spawning.
According to Wikipedia, 3–50 weakly sticky eggs are scattered over the substrate without guarding, and the parents may eat them.
Wikipedia says spawning takes about 100 minutes and eggs hatch about a week later.
According to Wikipedia, the young take about a year to reach adulthood.
In aquaria, the male clamps onto the female's underside until she releases her eggs.
